rationale: The BOOK ENTRY's core claim—that meat symbolizes the word obeyed to completeness rather than more advanced doctrinal content—is carried directly by the cited texts. John 4:34 is an explicit, in-text definition from Jesus himself ('My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work'), and 'to finish his work' supplies the 'to completeness' modifier. The Matt 12:50/Luke 8:21 parallel establishes 'do the will' = 'hear the word of God, and do it,' and Ps 40:8 gives the same equation ('do thy will... thy law is within my heart'), grounding 'the word... carried through to complete obedience.' Heb 5:14 attributes meat-eating maturity to 'reason of use' (practice), not to reception of harder content, and supplies verbatim the entry's 'exercising the senses to discern.' John 7:17 makes doing the will the precondition of knowing doctrine, and Job 34:3 links testing words to tasting meat. The strongest counter—meat as advanced teaching for the mature—cannot explain John 4:34 as anything but a disconnected second sense, cannot explain John 6:55 at all under its own definition, and must read Heb 5:14's 'by reason of use' as incidental. The book's reading unifies every cited text under one referent with an explicit scriptural definition; the counter fragments the evidence into unrelated senses. Under inference to the best explanation of the supplied case, the book wins, and every material assertion printed in the entry is supported.
book_core_identification: Meat symbolizes the word of God obeyed—doing the Father's will—carried through to completion, as opposed to merely receiving the word; i.e., milk and meat are one substance (the word) in two states (received vs. done), not elementary vs. advanced content.
book_secondary_elaborations: Milk is the word received (the counterpart state of the same word).
Meat entails 'to completeness'—finishing the work, echoing John 4:34's 'and to finish his work.'
The meat state exercises the senses to discern (good and evil), per Hebrews 5:14.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's claim that the milk/fat consonantal ambiguity (חלב) in Ezekiel 34:3 doubles as an indictment of shepherds is a chapter-level argument not asserted in the entry.
The chapter's basar (flesh)/gospel-tidings Hebrew wordplay tying John 6:55 to 'the gospel is the meat' is an extra derivational step beyond the entry.

The chapter's reconciliation of 1 Corinthians 2:2/2:6/3:2 (same message, different state of eater) is a supporting argument for the entry, not part of it, and its handling of 'not able to bear it' could be contested at chapter level.
The chapter's stance on rejecting Masoretic vowel points as non-infallible is a methodological claim outside the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Meat (strong meat/solid food) symbolizes advanced or deeper spiritual teaching suited to mature believers, contrasted with milk as elementary doctrine for spiritual infants (Heb 5:12-14; 1 Cor 3:1-2). Under this reading, John 4:34 and John 6:55 are separate, unrelated uses of 'meat' (food generally; eucharistic flesh), not instances of the milk/meat symbol.
counter_core_identification: Meat = advanced doctrinal content (a difference in the teaching itself), given only to the spiritually mature.
material_core_denial: The counter asserts the milk/meat difference is a difference in the content of teaching (elementary vs. advanced doctrine); the book entry asserts it is a difference in the state of the same word (received vs. obeyed to completion). Both cannot be true of the same referent: if meat is simply the word done, it is not a distinct, harder body of doctrine, and vice versa.
counter_case: Hebrews 5:12-13 speaks of 'the first principles of the oracles of God' needing to be re-taught, which naturally suggests a curriculum of content stages, milk being basics and meat being what lies beyond them.

1 Corinthians 3:1-2 has Paul actively withholding meat ('ye were not able to bear it'), which is most naturally read as withholding certain teaching content, not withholding obedience, which a teacher cannot dispense.
This is the overwhelmingly dominant reading across published Christian interpretation (all four common-interpretation responses list it as primary), reflecting long exegetical consensus.
It treats John 4:34 and John 6:55 as independent idioms of 'meat'=food, which is lexically plausible in KJV English where 'meat' means food generally.
book_explanatory_advantages: John 4:34 is an explicit scriptural definition of the symbol from Jesus' own mouth—'My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work'—directly supplying both 'obeyed' and 'to completeness'; the counter must sever this verse from the symbol entirely.

Hebrews 5:14 grounds meat-maturity in 'reason of use' (practice/doing), not in reception of harder content, and its 'senses exercised to discern' is quoted verbatim in the entry; the counter treats this causal clause as incidental.

The Matt 12:50/Luke 8:21 double witness equates 'do the will of my Father' with 'hear the word of God, and do it,' converting 'the will done' into 'the word done'—precisely the entry's formula—corroborated by Ps 40:8.

John 7:17 makes obedience the epistemic key to doctrine ('If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine'), cohering with meat-as-obedience unlocking discernment; the counter has no use for this verse.

John 6:55 ('my flesh is meat indeed') is integrated by the book (the Word embodied and done, keyed by John 6:63's 'the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit'), whereas 'advanced teaching' cannot make Jesus' flesh a harder lecture.

The book's reading unifies all nine cited texts under one consistent referent, matching the book's stated method of symbols defined openly in one passage and used consistently elsewhere; the counter requires at least three unrelated senses of 'meat' across the same citation list.

Job 34:3 and the taste/test motif ('the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat') fits meat as word-to-be-tested-by-doing, and gives Matt 24:45 ('meat in due season') a coherent place as the word served to be done.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It reads Hebrews 5:12's 'first principles of the oracles of God' (not in the printed citations) most naturally as a content curriculum.
It explains 1 Corinthians 3:1-2's picture of a teacher choosing what to feed a congregation without needing the book's 'same message, different state of eater' harmonization.
It matches the settled consensus of published interpretation, minimizing interpretive novelty.
decisive_sources: John 4:34 — explicit definition: meat = doing the will and finishing the work (obedience to completeness).
Matthew 12:50 with Luke 8:21 — two-witness equation: the will done = the word heard and done.
Hebrews 5:14 — meat belongs to those matured 'by reason of use,' with senses exercised to discern; supplies the entry's discernment clause verbatim.
John 7:17 — doing the will is the condition for knowing the doctrine.
Psalm 40:8 — doing God's will identified with the law within the heart (the word).
Job 34:3 — words tried by the ear as meat is tasted, tying meat to tested/practiced word.
unresolved_objections: Hebrews 5:12-13 and 1 Corinthians 3:1-2 (the counter's home texts, partly outside the printed citations) retain a surface reading of content-staged teaching; the book's harmonization (same Christ served as milk to babes and wisdom to the perfect) is plausible but argued in the chapter rather than self-evident.
Matthew 24:45 ('meat in due season') is compatible with the entry but does not independently discriminate between the two readings.
The dominance of the advanced-teaching reading in interpretive tradition means the entry bears a novelty burden, though tradition-counting is not evidence under this experiment's standard.
